bib.title: From Static Templates to Dynamic Runtime Graphs: A Survey of Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "From Static Templates to Dynamic Runtime Graphs: A Survey of Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents", Ling Yue, Kushal Raj Bhandari, Ching-Yun Ko, Dhaval Patel, Shuxin Lin, Nianjun Zhou, Jianxi Gao, Pin-Yu Chen, Shaowu Pan (RPI and IBM Research). Preprint, arXiv:2603.22386v1 [cs.AI], 23 Mar 2026. The page-1 title differs from the expected one: the arXiv metadata title is "Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents", but the PDF title is the longer one above.

COVERAGE: 31 of 31 pages read (115,661 chars). The references (pp. 22-29) were skimmed only; the main text, appendix tables 6-9 and the A.2 coding rules were read in full. Figures were not extracted; the extraction has no captions beyond "Figure 1: An overview of workflow optimization for LLM Agents" (p. 4).

KEY POINT FOR THE TARGET NOTE: this is a conceptual survey. It reports NO experimental numbers (no accuracy, cost or latency results). Its only counts are the corpus sizes below. Every "when to use what" statement is the authors' synthesis, and they say so ("cross-paper empirical patterns rather than ... universal laws"). It does not use the words "supervisor" or "fan-out" as categories. The nearest terms are "manager-worker hierarchy", "communication pattern", "topology" and "parallel".

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Taxonomy axis. Static vs dynamic is decided by WHEN structure is fixed. Static means a reusable template fixed after training or search. Dynamic means some of the realized graph is constructed, selected or edited at inference time.
  number: none
  setup: two descriptors. Graph determination time (GDT) is offline, pre-execution or in-execution. Graph plasticity mode (GPM) is none, select, generate or edit.
  quote: "A method isstaticif its deployed structure is a reusable template whose structural degrees of freedom are fixed after training or search. The template can still contain conditional execution, loops, or stochasticity, but those behaviors are already encoded in the reusable scaffold."
  where: Sec 2.4.1, p.10
- claim: Gray cases. An offline-trained generator that emits a new graph per input is dynamic. A fixed super-graph with runtime pruning is dynamic. A pre-authored "retry once" branch is static.
  number: none
  setup: taxonomy rule
  quote: "a workflow generator trained offline but used to emit a new plan for each input is dynamic in our taxonomy, because the realized graph is determined pre-execution at inference time. Likewise, a fixed super-graph with inference-time pruning is meaningfully dynamic"
  where: Sec 2.4.2, p.10
- claim: Three objects are kept apart. The template is the reusable design (V,E,Φ,Σ,A). The realized graph is the structure used in one run. The trace is the states, actions, observations and costs of that run. Every run has a realized graph; dynamic means some of it is chosen at inference time.
  number: none
  setup: Definitions 1-3, Sec 2.2, p.8
  quote: "a method is dynamic not because such a graph exists, but because some of its structure is chosen or revised at inference time rather than being fully fixed in the reusable template."
  where: p.8
- claim: Agentic computation graph (ACG) abstraction. Nodes are atomic actions (LLM call, retrieval, tool, validation, message passing). Edges are control, data or communication dependencies. In multi-agent systems, agents are nodes and messages are edges. A scheduler or router decides what runs next, what runs in parallel, when to stop and whether to replan.
  number: none
  setup: framing
  quote: "many workflows also include a scheduler or router that decides which node executes next, which nodes can run in parallel, when to terminate, and whether replanning is allowed."
  where: Sec 2.1, p.6
- claim: Dynamic plasticity forms a three-step spectrum: select/prune on a fixed super-graph, then pre-execution generation, then in-execution editing. The design rule is to use the minimum plasticity the task needs. Each step right adds validation, stopping and budget burden.
  number: none
  setup: synthesis from the surveyed papers
  quote: "dynamic methods should be selected based on the minimum structural plasticity required by the workload. Selection is often the right first step when tasks vary mostly in difficulty or communication budget. Generation becomes worthwhile when different tasks require genuinely different workflow structures. Editing is best reserved for environments where runtime observations materially change what the workflow ought to do next."
  where: Sec 7.2, p.20
- claim: Selection and pruning of a super-graph is the lightest dynamism. Validity is inherited from the super-graph, and it often captures much of the cost savings. It cannot add a missing verifier, tool or decomposition.
  number: none
  setup: Adaptive Graph Pruning, DAGP, AgentDropout, DyLAN, MasRouter, SkillOrchestra. No savings figure is given.
  quote: "A pruning policy cannot introduce a missing verifier, a missing tool, or a new decomposition strategy if the super-graph never contained those options."
  where: Sec 4.1, p.14
- claim: Static is enough when the operator space is constrained, the evaluator is trustworthy and the workload is repetitive. A well-searched template can then beat ad hoc runtime generation on cost and debuggability. Static's weakness is that it cannot tell the current input needs a different design (tool drift, shift, heterogeneous tasks).
  number: none
  setup: examples given are code generation with unit tests and hardware (Verilog) generation
  quote: "a well-searched template can dominate ad hoc runtime generation because it is cheaper, easier to debug, and easier to benchmark."
  where: Sec 7.1, pp.18-19
- claim: Practical hybrid recipe. Start with a constrained static scaffold plus node-level prompt optimization. Add graph search only when traces show structural failures. Prefer runtime selection or pruning before generation. Reserve editing for high environmental uncertainty. Finally sparsify communication.
  number: none
  setup: authors' synthesis, "not universal"
  quote: "Add graph-level search only when trace analysis reveals structural failure modes rather than purely local instruction errors. Under heterogeneous deployment conditions, prefer runtime selection or pruning before full workflow generation."
  where: Sec 7.5, p.21
- claim: Prompt tuning does not replace missing structure. If the wrong node ran, the right node never existed, or the information path was wrong, fix the graph. Inspect traces before optimizing prompts.
  number: none
  setup: cites Multi-Agent Design (Zhou 2025) and Maestro (Wang 2025a)
  quote: "A useful practical heuristic is to inspect traces before optimizing prompts: if the error arises because the wrong node executed, the right node never existed, or the information path was wrong, a better prompt is unlikely to be the real fix."
  where: Sec 7.3, p.20
- claim: Dynamic control needs guard machinery that counts as part of the workflow policy. This includes token, tool-call and time caps, stopping rules, fallbacks, and loop avoidance (repeated-state detection, edit caps).
  number: none
  setup: applies to in-execution editing
  quote: "loop-avoidance mechanisms such as repeated-state detection or edit caps. These are not minor engineering details. They are part of the workflow policy itself"
  where: Sec 7.2, p.20
- claim: Counter-evidence on multi-agent value. OneFlow argues some multi-agent gains can be reproduced by one strong single-agent simulator when roles share a backbone and reuse context.
  number: none
  setup: reported second-hand; the survey did not run it
  quote: "some gains attributed to multi-agent workflows can be reproduced by a strong single-agent simulator when roles share the same backbone and can reuse context efficiently."
  where: Sec 7.5, p.21
- claim: Verifiers pay off most when cheap and semantically meaningful (unit tests, schema, executability, synthesizability). Place them before expensive downstream steps. Strong verifiers allow more aggressive mutation.
  number: none
  setup: qualitative synthesis
  quote: "The design question is therefore not merely whether to use a verifier, but where to place it and how often to invoke it."
  where: Sec 7.4, p.20
- claim: Corpus size of the survey (the only hard numbers).
  number: 77 in-scope works (39 core, 7 adjacent, 31 background); 27 evaluation assets (20 benchmark or environment papers, 7 dataset or validator resources)
  setup: authors' inventory, scope rules in Sec 1
  quote: "we compiled an inventory of 77 in-scope works, including 39corepapers, 7adjacentpapers, and 31backgroundresources."
  where: Sec 1, p.5
- claim: Quality-cost objective. Maximize E[R(τ;x) − λC(τ)] over inputs, realized graphs and traces.
  number: none (schematic)
  setup: Eq. 1, "schematic"
  quote: "maxE x∼D [ EGrun|x [ Eτ|G run,x [R(τ;x)−λC(τ)] ]]"
  where: Sec 2.3, p.8
- claim: Reporting protocol. Papers should report the workflow used, how it varied and what it cost. For static templates, report size, depth, width, critical path length and communication volume. For dynamic methods, report edit count, fraction of steps spent editing, and structural variance across samples or paraphrases. Use cost-per-success. Table 5 lists 9 reporting dimensions.
  number: none
  setup: proposal; not a measured result
  quote: "workflow papers should not report onlywhat answer was produced. They should also reportwhat workflow was used, how that workflow varied across instances, and what it cost to obtain it."
  where: Sec 6.2-6.3, p.18
- claim: Feedback signals decide safe action granularity. Strong verifiers allow aggressive mutation. Preferences stabilize generation when scalar rewards are noisy. Textual feedback is a proposer, and metrics or verifiers should decide.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 5
  quote: "In the strongest systems, textual feedback acts as a proposal mechanism, while metrics or verifiers decide whether the proposal should survive."
  where: Sec 5.4, p.16

TAXONOMY (for the note)
- Static (GDT offline, GPM none). Three levels by optimization target: node (prompts, models in a fixed scaffold: DSPy, OPRO, EvoPrompt, CAPO, GEPA, Optima), graph (AFlow, ADAS, A2Flow, SEW, VFlow, MermaidFlow, Evolutionary Generation of MAS), joint (MASS / Multi-Agent Design, Maestro, Hu 2024 differentiable communication graph).
- Dynamic, three GPM modes.
  - Select (pre-exec): Adaptive Graph Pruning, DAGP, AgentDropout, DyLAN, MasRouter, SkillOrchestra, Difficulty-Aware Orchestration. The last of these is tagged pre-exec / select in Table 3.
  - Generate (pre-exec): Assemble Your Crew (autoregressive DAG), G-Designer (VGAE), graph diffusion (Jiang 2025), MaAS (agentic supernet), ScoreFlow, FlowReasoner, Workflow-R1, AutoFlow, WorkflowLLM, RobustFlow, ComfyUI-R1.
  - Edit (in-exec): DyFlow, AgentConductor, Aime, AOrchestra, MetaGen, ProAgent, Flow, EvoFlow, DebFlow, QualityFlow. AutoAgents is hybrid (draft, then edit).
- Orthogonal axes: optimization target (node, graph, joint), evidence (metric, verifier, preference, trace, plus supervision and proxy in the tables) and update mechanism (search, generator, controller, RL, preference optimization, repair/edit, continuous relaxation, hybrid).
- Table 2 and Table 3 give a per-method card (GDT/GPM, level, representation, feedback, update, cost handling).
- Representation types: code, text, DSL, JSON/YAML, typed operator graph, constrained IR (Mermaid).
- Frameworks and baselines (Table 8): CAMEL, AutoGen, EvoAgentX, MacNet (DAG collaboration), OpenHands, OneFlow.

LIMITS
- No new experiments, no pooled numbers, no cost or accuracy comparisons across methods. Guidance is from the authors' reading of the papers.
- The authors concede the claims are patterns, not laws: "cross-paper empirical patterns rather than ... universal laws"; "This recipe is not universal".
- The survey is a snapshot of a fast-moving field. It excludes planning-only and tool-use-only papers, and the inventory is "in-scope", not exhaustive.
- Open problems it names: structural credit assignment; expressivity vs verifiability; adaptation under tool or API drift (very few papers report adaptation efficiency); benchmark and evaluator quality; no theory of when dynamic generation is necessary.
- Most surveyed benchmarks are not structure-aware (Table 4 marks interactive tool-use and software benchmarks as ×).
- It says little about the classic named patterns (supervisor/orchestrator-worker, fan-out/map-reduce, handoff). Topology is treated as optimized graph structure, not as a pattern catalogue. The only supervisor-like mentions are "manager-worker hierarchy" (p.4), Aime's planner plus actor factory, and AOrchestra's sub-agent creation as a callable action.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025e); ADAS (Hu et al., 2025a); DSPy (Khattab et al., 2023); OPRO (Yang et al., 2023); EvoPrompt (Guo et al., 2023); GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025); MASS / Multi-Agent Design (Zhou et al., 2025); MacNet (Qian et al., 2025); AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023); CAMEL (Li et al., 2023a); G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025d); MaAS (Zhang et al., 2025b); Adaptive Graph Pruning (Li et al., 2025a). Prior surveys it positions against (Table 1): Yu et al. 2025, Li et al. 2024a, Huang et al. 2024, Xu et al. 2025b, Chen et al. 2024b, Tran et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2025f, Du et al. 2026, V et al. 2026.

CODE: none. The paper has no code. A companion list is at github.com/IBM/awesome-agentic-workflow-optimization (p.1).

FIGURES: Figure 1 (p.4), "An overview of workflow optimization for LLM Agents". It was not extracted and I did not view it. Tables 2 and 3 (pp.9 and 12) are the most useful single artefact, giving the per-method static/dynamic comparison cards. Table 5 (p.19) is the reporting checklist.

PROBLEMS: Text extraction is clean apart from run-together words (for example "andλcontrols"). Table cells are linearised, so column alignment is inferred (the Table 3 row order was cross-checked against the surrounding prose). No embedded instructions were found. The title differs from the one you expected (see SOURCE). The PDF is v1 only.
